tags.gist: Summarizes its proposal: the authorized device system, not the model, is the unit of assurance, with deterministic safety enforcement, assurance cases and bounded autonomy.
Wants competency evaluation combined with an auditable assurance case binding configuration, authority boundaries, operational evidence, exchanges, signals and change decisions.
Appreciates CDRH's early engagement and supports a risk-proportionate, least-burdensome approach.
Supports the two-axis heuristic and competency approach and agrees on evaluating the configured device, asking that this focus extend across the lifecycle.

Recommends nine principles, including risk modifiers, trajectory evaluation, deterministic safety invariants, versioned assurance cases, identity controls, an AI bill of materials and data governance.
Proposes a technology-neutral auditable lifecycle assurance framework specifying the minimum relationships that must stay provable across the lifecycle.
Argues trust needs proof of what acted under whose authority, calling for probabilistic intelligence under deterministic governance, compatible with existing QMS and PCCP practice.
Asks FDA to coordinate with HHS civil rights, health IT and consumer protection authorities where they hold primary authority, to avoid conflicting requirements.
Says location is an unreliable boundary and wants the device function characterized by purpose, recipient, personalization, directiveness, review opportunity, authority, time to harm and persistence.
Offers five illustrative classes, from device-contained assistance to distributed clinical AI systems, each with a boundary-defining characteristic and assurance focus.
Says a cloud or subscription service may hold a device function if its intended use is medical, while hospital use alone does not.
Illustrates how a check-in service becomes a device function once it uses patient-specific data to classify risk or triage, wanting that boundary defined, not emergent.
Illustrates how a hospital copilot crosses into device territory when it analyzes patterns, makes unreviewable recommendations or directs time-sensitive action.
Illustrates how an orchestration service becomes action-taking software once it changes thresholds, adjusts therapy or sends control commands.
Wants sponsors able to validate bounded functions inside a broader service while nominally non-device features are kept from becoming diagnostic through personalization or tools.
Asks FDA to clarify which hospital configuration changes remain deployment settings, which modify a device function, who validates the integration, and how evidence is exchanged.
Lists scope questions: what makes a hospital assistant a device function, how the responsible boundary is set among organizations, and when local configuration needs review.
Keeps the two axes for inherent risk but adds a modifier profile: reversibility, time to harm, independent oversight, traceability, state persistence, exposure and uncertainty visibility.
Wants directiveness judged across trajectories, with intended use describing permitted trajectory classes, prohibited transitions and when human review becomes mandatory.
Wants longitudinal conversations tested that cross scope gradually, including adversarial, manipulative and incomplete inputs.
Wants under- and over-escalation measured against separate clinically justified thresholds rather than one accuracy score.
Wants patient-facing status treated as a context modifier, not a presumption of unacceptable risk, with agency preserved through calibrated uncertainty and real handoff.
Supports benchmarking then confirmation, provided every result is tied to one uniquely identified configuration, since unbound scores are not reproducible.
Wants reliability shown as a bounded outcome distribution through repeated tests, with error frequencies, bounds and severity, plus scenario coverage for rare catastrophic hazards.
Wants statistical evidence paired with safety invariants enforced outside the model, such as scope prohibitions and authenticated approvals, since prompts are not deterministic controls.
Wants a cross-cutting assurance-integrity element checking configuration, evidence, runtime and change integrity under operation, failure, attack and change.

Wants benchmark validity shown through a documented package covering construct, coverage, contamination, subgroup representation and adjudicator agreement, with sequestered assets for high-consequence claims.
Wants the confirmation method to depend on whether the device assists a human, directs action or acts on its own.
Wants team performance as comparator when the team is the intended use, and autonomous performance where human review is not effective.
Wants synthetic data to supplement, not erase, evidence from representative distributions, especially for rare events and groups that are underrepresented.
Supports third parties for sequestered assets, adversarial testing, adjudication and integrity verification, with disclosed conflicts and no exclusive certification structures.
Would allow more postmarket reliance only with prespecified signals, thresholds, escalation, pause authority and coverage evidence, not for autonomous or irreversible actions.
Wants observability proportionate and privacy preserving, emphasizing configuration identifiers and control interventions over wholesale retention of prompts and records.
Wants an explicit lifecycle for data GenAI creates, covering purpose, access, retention, correction, secondary use and suppliers, preserving enough evidence to investigate failures.
Wants reassessment both periodic and event-triggered, with triggers from model, prompt, tool or site changes to drift, cybersecurity events and complaint patterns.
Wants supervisors with narrower roles, diverse implementation, restricted privileges and validated detection, warning that the same model family reviewing itself is not supervision.
Welcomes ecosystem signals and adjudication while the manufacturer keeps aggregation, triage, corrective action and reporting, under data-sharing agreements.
Wants consequential information exchanges across hospitals, clouds and providers to carry identity, purpose, scope, provenance and integrity, with evidence properties specified, not technologies.
Wants changes classified by affected competency, hazard, control and population rather than component type, with a baseline defining the re-evaluation set per impact pathway.
Says PCCPs can define change envelopes, triggers, evidence modules, thresholds and rollback criteria even when future model weights are unknown.
Wants provider contracts with notice, pinning, prior-version access and incident cooperation, technical detection of unannounced changes, and an exit strategy.
Finds a master file useful if versioned and contractually referenced, lists contents, and wants tiered disclosure protecting proprietary detail.
Wants the master file to feed, not replace, a sponsor-maintained AI bill of materials covering model, prompts, retrieval, tools, policies, evidence and change lineage.
Wants a declared authority envelope, verifiable identities, authenticated checkpoints for irreversible actions, least-privilege tools, containment and multi-step failure testing.
Describes the assurance case as a versioned argument linking intended use to hazards, controls, tests, configuration, deployment evidence, signals and changes.
Sets out a minimum identity and provenance graph relating device, configuration, competency, actors, runtime events, signals and changes.
Proposes a supplemental AI bill of materials layered on existing product and cybersecurity records, covering model, data, configuration, tools, evidence and data-governance layers.
Proposes an exchange envelope for distributed functions carrying sender, purpose, schema, provenance and outcome, with control commands protected more strongly than observations.
Proposes eight lifecycle gates from scope and configuration through competency, deployment, runtime, signal, change and retirement.
Wants consequential events reconstructable, including who acted, which versions and policies applied, what was authorized or reversed, and how data was handled, without hoarding records.
Illustrates evidence depth rising from baseline for non-directive uses to independent supervision and sequestered testing for autonomous high-consequence ones.
Suggests outcome metrics such as time to escalation, boundary adherence across turns, calibration, tool accuracy, checkpoint compliance and time to detect and correct.
Wants the framework implemented incrementally, reusing existing design, risk, cybersecurity and PCCP evidence, with modular updates and a multi-stakeholder pilot.
Calls competency assessment a strong foundation that must be tied into an assurance case that stays auditable, to survive change and autonomy.
Recommends FDA test the assurance framework through open workshops and a voluntary pilot covering AI bills of materials and privacy-preserving observability.
